## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.85596.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.85596.3.sa1)

In this manuscript, the authors used an unbiased method to identify proteins from porcine oocyte extracts associated with permeabilised boar spermatozoa in vitro. The identification of the proteins is done by mass spectrometry. A previous publication of this lab validated the cell-free extract purification methods as recapitulating early events after sperm entry in the oocyte. This novel method with mammalian gametes has the advantage that it can be done with many spermatozoa at the time and allows the identification of proteins associated with many permeabilised boar spermatozoa at the time. This allowed the authors to establish a list of proteins either enriched or depleted after incubation with the oocytes extract or even only associated with spermatozoa after incubation for 4h or 24h. The total number of proteins identified in their test is around 200 and with very few present in the sample only when spermatozoa were incubated with the extracts.

The list of proteins identified using this approach and these criteria provide a list of proteins likely associated with spermatozoa remnants after their entry and either removed or recruited for the transformation of spermatozoa-derived structures. Using WB and histochemistry labelling of spermatozoa and early embryos using specific antibodies the authors confirmed the association/dissociation of 6 proteins suspected to be involved in autophagy.

While this unique approach provides a list of potential proteins involved in sperm mitochondria clearance it is (only) a starting point for many future studies and does not provide the demonstration that any of these proteins has indeed a role in the processes leading to sperm mitochondria clearance. The protein identified may also be involved in other processes going on in the oocyte at this time of early development.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.85596.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.85596.3.sa2)

Mitochondria are essential cellular organelles that generate ATPs as the energy source for maintaining regular cellular functions. However, the degradation of sperm-borne mitochondria after fertilization is a conserved event known as mitophagy to ensure the exclusively maternal inheritance of the mitochondrial DNA genome. Defects on post-fertilization sperm mitophagy will lead to fatal consequences in patients. Therefore, understanding the cellular and molecular regulation of the post-fertilization sperm mitophagy process is critically important. In this study, Zuidema et. al applied mass spectrometry in conjunction with a porcine cell-free system to identify potential autophagic cofactors involved in post-fertilization sperm mitophagy. They identified a list of 185 proteins that might be candidates for mitophagy determinants (or their co-factors). Despite the fact that 6 (out of 185) proteins were further studied, based on their known functions, using a porcine cell-free system in conjunction with immunocytochemistry and Western blotting, to characterize the localization and modification changes these proteins, no further functional validation experiments were performed. Nevertheless, the data presented in the current study is of great interest and could be important for future studies in this field.

results.result: Mass spectrometry analysis of the porcine cell-free system identified 185 proteins with statistically different abundances (p<0.1) between control and cell-free-treated spermatozoa across two time points (4 hr and 24 hr). The 4 hr trial identified 144 proteins and the 24 hr trial identified 63 proteins, with 22 proteins overlapping between trials.
results.evaluation: The mass spectrometry methodology is clearly described with appropriate biological replicates (n=3 per trial), normalization procedures (based on outer dense fiber proteins), and statistical analysis (paired T-test). The quantitative results are internally consistent and the experimental design is sound for a discovery-based proteomics study.

results.result: Proteins were classified into three functional classes based on their abundance patterns: Class 1 (ooplasmic proteins binding to sperm), Class 2 (sperm proteins increasing after extract exposure), and Class 3 (sperm proteins decreasing after extract exposure).
results.evaluation: The classification system is logical and well-defined based on protein abundance patterns. The interpretations of each class (C67, C70) are reasonable given the experimental design, though they remain hypotheses requiring further validation.

results.result: Class 1 proteins included well-documented oocyte-specific proteins (zona pellucida proteins 2, 3, 4; ovastacin; DNA methyltransferase 1; nucleoplasmin 2) that are known to interact with spermatozoa during fertilization, validating the cell-free system's ability to recapitulate fertilization events.
results.evaluation: The identification of known oocyte-specific proteins in Class 1 provides strong validation of the experimental system. These proteins are well-established in the literature as oocyte-specific and involved in fertilization, supporting the claim that the cell-free system recapitulates relevant biological interactions.

results.result: Several autophagy-related proteins (L-lactate dehydrogenase B chain, keratin 8, glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta 5, BAG5, SAMM50, FUNDC2) and multiple ubiquitin-proteasome system components were identified in the protein inventory, suggesting their involvement in post-fertilization sperm mitophagy.
results.evaluation: While these proteins were identified in the mass spectrometry data, the claim that they are mitophagy regulators (C129) or involved in UPS-mediated mitophagy (C131) is speculative. The mass spectrometry data shows abundance changes but does not demonstrate functional roles in mitophagy.

results.result: MVP was not detected in ejaculated or primed spermatozoa but was detected on sperm tails after 4 and 24 hr of cell-free system exposure. In zygotes, MVP was abundant in cytoplasm at 15 hr post-insemination without clear mitochondrial sheath association, but showed colocalization with the mitochondrial sheath at 25 hr post-insemination.
results.evaluation: The experimental observations are well-documented with both Western blotting and immunocytochemistry (Figures 3A-G). The temporal progression of MVP localization is clearly demonstrated, though the functional significance remains speculative.

results.result: PSMG2 significantly increased in abundance after 24 hr in the cell-free system (p=0.088) and showed dynamic localization changes: from acrosome in ejaculated sperm, to head and tail after 4 hr cell-free exposure, to head only after 24 hr, and finally clustering around paternal pronuclei and mitochondrial sheaths in zygotes at 25 hr post-insemination.
results.evaluation: The localization patterns are well-documented with immunocytochemistry (Figures 4A-G) and consistent with the known role of proteasome assembly chaperones. The p-value of 0.088 is marginally significant by the study's criteria (p<0.1), and the biological observations support the mass spectrometry findings.

results.result: PSMA3 significantly increased (p=0.015) during the 4 hr trial and localized to the acrosome in ejaculated sperm, then redistributed to the tail after priming and cell-free exposure, with increasing focus on the mitochondrial sheath over time. In zygotes, PSMA3 clustered around pronuclei and on mitochondrial sheaths at both 15 and 25 hr post-insemination.
results.evaluation: The statistical significance is strong (p=0.015) and the immunocytochemistry data (Figures 5A-G) clearly demonstrate the described localization patterns. The observations are consistent with the known role of proteasome subunits in post-fertilization events.

results.result: FUNDC2 significantly decreased in abundance after 4 hr of cell-free exposure (p=0.084) and showed complex localization dynamics: from acrosome and mitochondrial sheath in ejaculated sperm, to throughout the tail after 4 hr cell-free exposure, back to mitochondrial sheath with fractured pattern after 24 hr. FUNDC2 was not detected on fertilizing spermatozoa in zygotes but remained on zona-bound spermatozoa.
results.evaluation: The experimental observations are well-documented (Figures 6A-J). The decrease in abundance is statistically significant by the study's criteria. The differential localization between fertilizing and non-fertilizing spermatozoa is particularly interesting and well-demonstrated.

results.result: SAMM50 significantly decreased in abundance during the 4 hr trial (p=0.035) and localized to acrosome and mitochondrial sheath in ejaculated sperm. After cell-free exposure, acrosomal SAMM50 was removed while mitochondrial sheath localization persisted. In zygotes, SAMM50 localized on/near mitochondrial sheaths at 15 hr but shifted to the principal piece by 25 hr post-insemination.
results.evaluation: The statistical significance is strong (p=0.035) and the immunocytochemistry data (Figures 7A-G) clearly show the described patterns. The temporal dynamics in both cell-free system and zygotes are well-documented.

results.result: BAG5 decreased in abundance during the 4 hr trial (p=0.02) and was localized exclusively to the acrosome in ejaculated sperm. After cell-free exposure, BAG5 relocated to the mitochondrial sheath at both 4 and 24 hr. In zygotes, BAG5 was not observed on fertilizing spermatozoa but was present in the cytoplasm at both 15 and 25 hr post-insemination.
results.evaluation: The statistical significance is strong (p=0.02) and the immunocytochemistry data (Figures 8A-G) clearly demonstrate the localization changes. The removal of BAG5 from fertilizing spermatozoa is consistent with its proposed role in regulating mitophagy.

results.result: The porcine cell-free system was designed to recapitulate early fertilization proteomic interactions by combining oocyte extracts with primed spermatozoa. The system offers advantages over other models including the use of mammalian gametes, favorable timing of mitophagy, and the ability to observe thousands of spermatozoa simultaneously.
results.evaluation: The cell-free system design is well-justified with appropriate citations to prior work (C35, C45). The practical advantages are clearly articulated (C36-C39, C44) and the system has been previously validated. However, the authors acknowledge limitations (C121, C122) that the system does not perfectly capture all in vivo events.

results.result: The study has several acknowledged limitations: the cell-free system does not perfectly capture all in vivo fertilization events, protein losses occur during sample preparation, only protein abundance changes are captured (not localization or post-translational modifications), and the lack of overlap between 4 hr and 24 hr inventories may reflect inability to detect dynamic changes.
results.evaluation: The authors appropriately acknowledge the limitations of their experimental system and analytical approach. These are reasonable and honest assessments of the study's constraints.

results.result: The majority of protein changes observed were reductions in sperm protein content (75% at 4 hr, 68% at 24 hr), consistent with the known recycling of sperm structures (mitochondrial sheath, tail proteins, acrosome remnants, perinuclear theca) after fertilization while retaining essential components (DNA, centriole, mRNAs, proteins).
results.evaluation: The quantitative observations (C140, C141) are clearly stated and the interpretation (C142) is logical. The biological context provided by citations (C143-C145) supports the interpretation that sperm structure recycling explains the predominance of Class 3 proteins.

results.result: The mass spectrometry trial captured the majority of chaperone-independent alpha subunits (PSMA2 and PSMA3) and half of the complex regulating dependent alpha subunits (PSMG2), all increasing in abundance, confirming that proteasome assembly pathways are active in the cell-free system with likely contributions from both sperm-borne and ooplasm-derived components.
results.evaluation: The observation about capturing specific proteasome components (C170) is supported by the data (C84, C169). The inference that proteasome assembly pathways are active (C171) is reasonable, though the speculation about combined sperm and ooplasm contributions (C172) is less certain.

results.result: The depletion of SAMM50 from extract-exposed spermatozoa may allow PINK1-Parkin-mediated mitophagy to degrade sperm mitochondria, potentially linking this well-known somatic cell pathway to post-fertilization sperm mitophagy. SAMM50 may also interact with SQSTM1 in basal mitophagy to degrade mitochondrial complexes without replacement during programmed mitophagy.
results.evaluation: While the SAMM50 depletion is well-documented (C101-C107) and the cited literature on PINK1-Parkin and basal mitophagy is accurate (C184, C188-C190), the proposed mechanisms (C185, C187, C191) are highly speculative. The PINK1-Parkin pathway has not been documented in zygotic mitophagy (C186), making these interpretations uncertain.

results.result: Three alternative hypotheses are proposed for FUNDC2's role: (1) its removal could initiate an apoptotic cascade targeting sperm structures, (2) it could play an undescribed role in initiating sperm mitophagy, or (3) it may be a carryover protein from spermatogenesis that undergoes degradation along with other mitochondrial proteins.
results.evaluation: These are explicitly speculative hypotheses (C178-C180) presented as alternatives. While the experimental observations of FUNDC2 dynamics are solid (C91-C100), there is no data in this study to distinguish between these mechanistic possibilities.

results.result: In the context of post-fertilization sperm mitophagy, the pro-selective mitophagy BAG5 regulated pathway would be favored, and the early removal of BAG5 from fertilizing spermatozoa is likely promoting post-fertilization sperm mitophagy.
results.evaluation: While the BAG5 removal is well-documented (C108-C114) and the cited literature on BAG5's role in PINK1-Parkin regulation is accurate (C192-C200), the claim that BAG5 removal promotes mitophagy (C203) is speculative. No functional experiments were performed to test this hypothesis.

results.result: The study used unconventional statistical thresholds: p<0.2 for Class 1 proteins and p<0.1 for Class 2 and 3 proteins.
results.evaluation: The use of p<0.2 as a significance threshold for Class 1 proteins is unusually permissive and not well-justified. While the authors explain that Class 1 proteins were only found after cell-free exposure, this relaxed threshold increases the risk of false positives. Standard practice would use p<0.05 or at most p<0.1 uniformly.

results.result: This mass spectrometry study is claimed to be the first of its kind, and the porcine cell-free system will remain a useful tool to explore early fertilization events at the molecular level.
results.evaluation: The claim of novelty (C204) appears reasonable given the unique combination of the porcine cell-free system with quantitative mass spectrometry for studying fertilization proteomics. The conclusion about future utility (C205) is a reasonable inference based on the demonstrated capabilities of the system.

results.result: The porcine cell-free system recapitulates early fertilization proteomic interactions. The system was adapted from Xenopus laevis egg extracts and uses porcine oocytes matured in vitro combined with permeabilized boar spermatozoa. The authors claim this system mimics events that occur during natural fertilization and has been previously validated.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept the validity of the cell-free system approach. Reviewer 1 states 'A previous publication of this lab validated the cell-free extract purification methods as recapitulating early events after sperm entry in the oocyte.' Reviewer 3 is 'very positive about the porcine cell-free assay approach and the results presented here.' The editor notes 'The main method used is state-of-the-art and the supporting data are solid.'

results.result: Mass spectrometry analysis identified 185 proteins that showed statistically significant differences (p<0.1) between control and cell-free-treated spermatozoa across two time points (4 hr and 24 hr). The study used biological triplicates and normalized samples based on outer dense fiber protein content.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the mass spectrometry findings as valid. The editor states 'This important work reports the identification of a list of proteins that may participate in the clearance of paternal mitochondria.' Reviewer 1 notes 'The total number of proteins identified in their test is around 200' without questioning the methodology. Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'They identified a list of 185 proteins that might be candidates for mitophagy determinants.'

results.result: Proteins were classified into three classes based on their behavior in the cell-free system: Class 1 (oocyte-derived proteins binding to sperm), Class 2 (proteins increasing in abundance), and Class 3 (proteins decreasing in abundance). Class 1 included known oocyte-specific proteins such as zona pellucida proteins 2, 3, and 4, ovastacin, DNA methyltransferase 1, and nucleoplasmin 2.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the classification system and validation through known oocyte proteins. Reviewer 1 notes the system 'allowed the authors to establish a list of proteins either enriched or depleted after incubation with the oocytes extract.' The identification of known oocyte-specific proteins in Class 1 serves as internal validation that reviewers implicitly accept by not questioning it.

results.result: MVP (Major Vault Protein) was identified as a Class 1 protein, not detected in ejaculated or primed spermatozoa by Western blotting or immunocytochemistry, but detected on sperm tails after 4 and 24 hr of cell-free system exposure. In zygotes, MVP was abundant in cytoplasm at 15 hr post-insemination without associating with male pronuclei or mitochondrial sheaths, but showed colocalization with mitochondrial sheaths at 25 hr post-insemination.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the characterization of MVP. Reviewer 1 states 'Using WB and histochemistry labelling of spermatozoa and early embryos using specific antibodies the authors confirmed the association/dissociation of 6 proteins suspected to be involved in autophagy.' No specific concerns about MVP data are raised by any reviewer.

results.result: PSMG2 (Proteasome Assembly Chaperone 2) was identified as a Class 2 protein showing significant increase in abundance after 24 hr (p=0.088). It localized to the acrosome in ejaculated spermatozoa, appeared in both head and tail after 4 hr cell-free exposure, returned to head-only localization after 24 hr, and clustered around paternal pronuclei and on mitochondrial sheaths in zygotes at 15 and 25 hr post-insemination.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the PSMG2 characterization as part of the validated set of six proteins. Reviewer 1 confirms 'the authors confirmed the association/dissociation of 6 proteins suspected to be involved in autophagy' using appropriate methods. No specific methodological concerns about PSMG2 are raised.

results.result: PSMA3 (Proteasome Subunit Alpha 3) significantly increased (p=0.015) during 4 hr trials as a Class 2 protein. It localized to the acrosome in ejaculated spermatozoa, redistributed to the tail after priming and 4 hr cell-free exposure, showed more focused mitochondrial sheath localization after 24 hr, and clustered around pronuclei and on mitochondrial sheaths in zygotes at both 15 and 25 hr post-insemination.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the PSMA3 characterization. Reviewer 1 confirms validation of the six proteins through Western blotting and immunocytochemistry. The editor notes 'the supporting data are solid,' which encompasses these protein characterizations.

results.result: FUNDC2 (FUN14 Domain-Containing Protein 2) underwent significant decrease in abundance after 4 hr (p=0.084) as a Class 3 protein. It localized to acrosome and mitochondrial sheath in ejaculated spermatozoa, changed localization after capacitation and priming, spread throughout the tail after 4 hr cell-free exposure, returned to a fractured mitochondrial sheath pattern after 24 hr, and was not detected on fertilizing spermatozoa at 15 or 25 hr post-insemination but remained on zona-bound non-fertilizing sperm.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the FUNDC2 characterization. Reviewer 1 confirms the validation approach for all six proteins. The dynamic localization changes and disappearance from fertilizing sperm are not questioned by reviewers.

results.result: SAMM50 (Sorting and Assembly Machinery Component 50) showed significant decrease in abundance during 4 hr trial (p=0.035) as a Class 3 protein. It localized to acrosome and mitochondrial sheath in ejaculated spermatozoa, persisted on mitochondrial sheath and principal piece after priming and cell-free exposure (4 and 24 hr), localized on/near mitochondrial sheath at 15 hr post-insemination, but was detected only on principal piece (not mitochondrial sheath) at 25 hr post-insemination.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the SAMM50 characterization. Reviewer 1 confirms validation of all six proteins through appropriate methods. The temporal changes in localization are not questioned.

results.result: BAG5 (BAG Family Molecular Chaperone Regulator 5) decreased in abundance during 4 hr trial (p=0.02) as a Class 3 protein. It localized exclusively to the acrosome in ejaculated spermatozoa, was detectable in acrosome remains and weakly on tail after priming, relocated to mitochondrial sheath after 4 and 24 hr cell-free exposure, but was not observed on fertilizing spermatozoa at 15 or 25 hr post-insemination (though present in zygote cytoplasm).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the BAG5 characterization. Reviewer 1 confirms validation of all six proteins. The dramatic relocalization from acrosome to mitochondrial sheath and subsequent disappearance from fertilizing sperm are not questioned.

results.result: The 185 identified proteins likely play roles in multiple early fertilization processes beyond sperm mitophagy, including pronuclear development, sperm aster formation, and degradation of various sperm structures. Several autophagy-related proteins (FUNDC2, SAMM50, BAG5) and ubiquitin-proteasome system components were identified.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this limitation. Reviewer 1 states 'The protein identified may also be involved in other processes going on in the oocyte at this time of early development.' Reviewer 2 notes the proteins 'might be candidates for mitophagy determinants (or their co-factors),' indicating acceptance that not all proteins are directly mitophagy-related.

results.result: This mass spectrometry study represents the first comprehensive proteomic investigation of post-fertilization sperm mitophagy using the porcine cell-free system, identifying candidate proteins for future functional studies. The authors acknowledge that many protein cofactors and pathways remain to be identified.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recognize the study's value as a starting point but emphasize its limitations. Reviewer 1 states 'this unique approach provides a list of potential proteins involved in sperm mitochondria clearance it is (only) a starting point for many future studies and does not provide the demonstration that any of these proteins has indeed a role in the processes leading to sperm mitochondria clearance.' Reviewer 2 notes 'no further functional validation experiments were performed. Nevertheless, the data presented in the current study is of great interest and could be important for future studies in this field.'

results.result: The study captures changes in protein abundances only and would not detect proteins that remain at stable abundances but undergo changes in localization or post-translational modifications. The lack of overlap between 4 hr and 24 hr protein inventories may reflect inability to detect dynamic changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept these limitations by not challenging them. The authors' acknowledgment of these methodological constraints aligns with reviewers' understanding that this is a discovery-phase study providing candidate proteins rather than mechanistic proof.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on PSMG2 characterization (C76-C83). Both evaluations find the data SUPPORTED with appropriate Western blotting and immunocytochemistry methods. OpenEval notes the p=0.088 marginal significance while peer reviewers accept it without concern.

Perfect agreement on PSMA3 characterization (C84-C90). Both evaluations find the data SUPPORTED with strong statistical significance (p=0.015) and clear immunocytochemistry evidence. No methodological concerns raised by either evaluation.

Perfect agreement on FUNDC2 characterization (C91-C100). Both evaluations find the data SUPPORTED, noting the well-documented localization changes and differential behavior between fertilizing and non-fertilizing spermatozoa.

Perfect agreement on SAMM50 characterization (C101-C107). Both evaluations find the data SUPPORTED with strong statistical significance (p=0.035) and clear temporal dynamics demonstrated through immunocytochemistry.

Perfect agreement on BAG5 characterization (C108-C114). Both evaluations find the data SUPPORTED with strong statistical significance (p=0.02) and dramatic relocalization patterns clearly demonstrated.

Strong agreement on mass spectrometry methodology (C5-C7, C46-C65). Both find the approach SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes technical details (n=3 replicates, normalization, statistics) while peer reviewers focus on acceptance of the protein identification results (~185-200 proteins).

Perfect agreement on MVP characterization (C71-C75). Both evaluations find the data SUPPORTED with well-documented temporal progression through Western blotting and immunocytochemistry. OpenEval notes functional significance remains speculative.

Strong agreement on cell-free system validity (C34-C45). Both find the approach SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes practical advantages and prior validation while peer reviewers highlight acceptance by all reviewers and state-of-the-art methodology. Both acknowledge limitations (C121-C122).

Agreement on protein classification system (C66-C70). Both find it SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the system is logical and well-defined though interpretations remain hypotheses. Peer reviewers accept the classification for organizing enriched/depleted proteins.

Agreement on validation through known oocyte proteins (C133-C135). Both find this SUPPORTED as internal validation. OpenEval explicitly notes this validates the experimental system while peer reviewers implicitly accept by not questioning it.

Agreement on study limitations (C121-C125). Both find the authors' acknowledgment of limitations SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes these are reasonable assessments while peer reviewers implicitly accept them as appropriate for a discovery-phase study.

Divergence on mitophagy regulator claims (C128-C131). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting mass spectrometry shows abundance changes but not functional roles in mitophagy. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, explicitly acknowledging proteins 'might be candidates' and accepting the limitation that not all are directly mitophagy-related.

Divergence on novelty and utility claims (C204-C205). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, finding novelty reasonable and future utility justified. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, emphasizing this is 'only a starting point' and lacks functional validation, though data is 'of great interest.'

Potential disagreement on statistical threshold (C57). OpenEval rates UNSUPPORTED, criticizing p<0.2 as unusually permissive and increasing false positive risk. Peer reviewers rate mass spectrometry findings SUPPORTED without specifically addressing this statistical concern.
